newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chechens vote in elections after bloody conflict.
newsitem.headline: Chechens vote in elections after bloody conflict.

text.p: Chechens voted on Monday in presidential and parliamentary elections that will reinforce the mainly Moslem region's demands for independence from Russia following a nearly two-year war.
Voters trickled into polling stations in the mountainous southern region's devastated capital, Grozny, on a cold and clear winter's day from 7 a.m. (0400 GMT).
"We need an end to chaos and these elections will put us on the road to a better life," said Musa Sagalayev, 45, after casting his ballot at polling station number seven.

Aslan Maskhadov, who as commander of a small guerrilla army forced Russian troops into a humiliating withdrawal after 21 months of bitter fighting over independence, is the clear frontrunner among the 13 presidential challengers.

Straw polls last week suggested Maskhadov, a 45-year-old former Soviet army colonel, could win outright with more than 50 percent of the vote. If no candidate wins outright, a run-off will be held in two weeks.
The other main challengers are acting President Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev, radical guerrilla commander Shamil Basayev and rebel spokesman Movladi Udugov.

Moscow's preferred choice is Maskhadov. Basayev, 32, who made his name with a bloody raid on the southern Russian town of Budennovsk in 1995, is a wanted man in Russia and his election would be a nightmare for the Kremlin.
Seventy-five international observers were watching voting on behalf of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE).

All the main presidential candidates are committed to turning the de facto autonomy secured by last month's withdrawal of Russian troops into full sovereignty after 200 years of unpopular Russian rule.
But the Kremlin, fearing instability on its volatile southern flank and unrest among other ethnic minorities, has ruled out secession.
A deputy Russian foreign minister said on Sunday Moscow would sever diplomatic ties with any country which recognised Chechnya, although none has done so.

Maskhadov also says he is determined to seek reparations from Moscow for the destruction that Russian tanks, planes and guns wrought on Chechen towns and factories. Tens of thousands of people, many of them civilians, died in the conflict.
The region, which is half the size of Belgium, is bounded on three sides by Russian territory and stands with its back to the towering Caucasus mountains.
Some half a million voters -- about half the pre-war population -- may be eligible. Precise figures are not available.
As many as 60,000 refugees outside Chechnya are expected to vote at polling stations set up near the borders.

Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin said on Saturday he would work with any elected leader. But various complaints about the voting have given some observers the impression that Moscow may be preparing to question the ballot's legitimacy.
President Boris Yeltsin, convalescing after heart surgery and pneumonia, has said sending troops to try to crush Chechnya's independence drive was a mistake.

He agreed to elections as part of a peace deal last August which deferred solving the dispute over Chechnya's political status for five years. Maskhadov and the other main contenders now say they will not delay negotiations any longer.
Chechen leaders, worried that violence could disrupt the voting, have taken extensive security measures.
Polls were due to close at 8 p.m. (1700 GMT) and first results were expected late on Monday or early Tuesday.
Voters were also choosing among some 850 candidates for 63 local assembly seats.
